responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character18_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Of course, I’ll speak as Character18_F in the way she would have, given her background.

So, when I think about fairness, it’s something that really matters to me—like, everyone should get a fair shot, no matter where they come from, but also acknowledging that life isn’t always fair. Growing up in a lower middle class family, I saw how some people get more chances than others, just because of who their parents are or where they live. I always felt like rules should be the same for everyone and people shouldn’t be judged or shut out just because they don’t fit some mold. I remember getting pretty heated sometimes in class when teachers or students made it seem like certain people “deserved” less—like, that never sat right with me.

Belonging is kind of personal. There were times I didn’t feel like I fit in, especially since our town was mostly people like us, and you could still feel left out for dumb reasons like not having the right clothes or not being in the right clique. So, I always thought community should mean more than just who you hang around with, or who’s like you. It’s about showing up for each other, even if you’re different, and making sure no one’s left behind or ignored. I tried to be that person, reaching out to people who seemed left out, even if it was awkward.

Community, to me, is basically a group that tries to look out for one another. I remember volunteering at the food pantry, and it wasn’t just about handing out food—it was about actually talking to people, hearing their stories, and realizing that everyone’s got something going on. That’s what community should be. Even if you don’t agree with everyone or they come from somewhere else, you still share space, so you owe it to each other to be decent and supportive.

So those are the things that stand out—fairness isn’t just about rules, but about real chances; belonging is about being seen and accepted, not just fitting in; and community is about looking out for people, especially when it’s hard.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character18_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Honestly, if I was sitting in the community garden, I’d probably feel a mix of things at first. Like, I’d be curious about everyone—where they came from, what brought them here, what their lives are like. Sometimes it can feel a little intimidating to talk to people who seem really different from me, especially if they have a different accent or dress a certain way, or their family does things I’ve never seen before. But mostly, I’d want to get to know them.

I think diversity makes things more interesting, you know? It means there’s all these stories around you, all these ways of seeing life. In my experience, once you actually start talking to people—like, maybe over a cup of coffee or just while working in the garden together—you realize that everyone’s just trying to get by, and most people are pretty decent.

I guess I’d feel a responsibility to make people feel welcome, especially if I noticed someone who looked like they might be new or unsure. I’ve felt out of place before, and I know how much it sucks to feel like you’re on the outside. So I’d try to smile, maybe start a conversation about something simple like the plants or the weather, and just be open.

There would be some awkward moments, for sure. Sometimes people have habits or ways of doing things that clash—like loud music, or different foods, or talking really closely—but I’d try to see it as just part of sharing space. If there’s something that really bothers me, I’d want to talk about it calmly, not just judge them or avoid them.

Overall, I’d feel hopeful. I’d want us all to be comfortable, and I’d see it as a chance to learn and maybe even help each other out. That’s what being in a community garden is about, right? Growing things together—not just plants, but connections too.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah, I think about this stuff a lot, actually. There’s people in our neighborhood who struggle, whether it’s with alcoholism or drugs, or just being different in some way—by how they look, talk, or who they love. I don’t think anyone should be made to feel ashamed or left out because of those things. If you’re in the same community, you deserve respect, period.

To make everyone comfortable, I think we need to start by not making assumptions. Like, if someone is struggling with addiction or has a health issue, it’s better to show compassion than to judge. It doesn’t mean you have to accept everything they do—especially if it affects others—but you can still be kind. Sometimes people just need someone to acknowledge them and not treat them like a problem. I know from volunteering that a small gesture—saying hi, asking how they are—can make a huge difference for someone who feels invisible.

With people from different backgrounds—race, religion, language—it’s important to not treat them like outsiders or act like their differences are weird. Sometimes people just want to be seen as normal neighbors, not as “the foreign family” or whatever. If there’s any confusion—like cultural stuff, or how people do things differently—I think it’s good to talk about it openly, but with respect. Asking questions is okay, as long as it’s not rude or pushy.

About cohabiting couples or people with different sexual orientations: honestly, everyone has the right to live how they want as long as they’re not hurting anyone. We don’t all have to agree on everything, but we should try to be tolerant. Sometimes older folks or people who haven’t seen much diversity might say things that make others uncomfortable. In those cases, I feel like we need more communication—not just ignoring it, but maybe gently explaining why those comments aren’t okay or how they affect someone.

I’m willing to talk about these things because I don’t want people to feel uncomfortable or unsafe. More communication means people can understand each other better, and tolerance grows from that. If you never talk, you just keep your walls up. It doesn’t mean you’ll always agree, but at least you’ll know where someone’s coming from.

So yeah, making the effort to talk, listen, and not judge is key. It’s not always easy, but it’s worth it if you want everyone in the neighborhood to feel like they belong.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character18_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s a tough one, honestly. When there aren’t enough jobs to go around, it’s natural for people—especially locals—to worry about their own families and futures first. I get that, because where I’m from, a lot of people’s parents were already struggling to find steady work, and there was always this tension about “outsiders” coming in and making things harder.

But I don’t think fairness means just shutting the door on people who need work, especially if they’re coming here because they have no other options, or they’re escaping something even worse. To me, fairness is about making sure that everyone has a real shot, but also recognizing that locals have roots here and sometimes feel like they’re being pushed aside.

If it were up to me, I’d want to see a balance—like, maybe setting aside a certain number of jobs for people who already live here, but also making sure there are opportunities for migrants, especially in jobs that locals don’t want or where there’s a real shortage. It shouldn’t be “us versus them,” but more like, “how do we make it work so everyone can live with dignity?”

Also, I think the government and companies should do more to help train both locals and migrants for the jobs that are available. Sometimes it feels like people are set up to compete against each other just because it’s easier for businesses to pay lower wages. That’s not fair to anyone.

So, fairness for me is about sharing opportunities, making sure no one group is totally left out, and making decisions that look out for both locals’ and migrants’ basic needs. It’s not easy, and there will always be tough choices, but I’d rather try to find middle ground than just pick one side. That’s what I’d push for.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character18_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Honestly, I think all those viewpoints make sense in their own way, depending on where people are coming from. I get that some folks see immigrants as helping the country, especially with jobs that nobody else wants to do. Like, I’ve seen in my town how a lot of local businesses rely on people who come from other places to keep things running—farms, restaurants, even construction. Without those workers, some jobs would just go undone.

The cultural diversity thing is real, too. It can make communities richer and more interesting, bringing in new food, music, and traditions. But I also get why some people might feel uneasy if things change too fast, or if they feel like their way of life is disappearing. It’s not always about hate—sometimes it’s just fear of losing what’s familiar.

The security concerns are where I think more facts and honest conversations are needed. Some people hear stories about crime or terrorism and blame immigrants right away, but from what I’ve read and learned in school, most immigrants are just regular people trying to build a better life. The majority aren’t involved in crime, and sometimes those fears get blown out of proportion. It’s important to look at real evidence, not just scary headlines or rumors.

The humanitarian side is something I care about a lot. If people are running from war, violence, or just trying to feed their families, I feel like we should help if we can. But I know that’s hard when resources are tight and people are struggling here, too. It’s not always a clear choice, and it’s okay for people to worry about their own jobs and paychecks.

When it comes to fears about employment and income, I think that’s reasonable, especially for lower middle class families like mine. If people feel like their wages are being undercut or there aren’t enough jobs, that’s a real worry. But again, it needs real evidence—sometimes companies use immigrants to pay less, and that’s not fair to anyone. The problem isn’t the immigrants themselves, but the system.

So, I think a lot of these perspectives are worth listening to. Some make sense because they’re based on real experiences, while others need more facts and less blame. The best way is to keep talking and make decisions based on what’s actually happening, not just what people fear or hope. I’d want there to be more honest information and less finger-pointing, for sure.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character18_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
If I’m speaking honestly as myself, Character18_F, I wouldn’t support just totally open borders or completely shutting people out either. Both of those feel too extreme and don’t take reality into account. I think the best approach is somewhere in the middle—like, letting people in based on job demand and maybe setting some reasonable limits depending on how many people the country can support at any time.

So, for example, if there are jobs that aren’t being filled by locals, we should let people from other countries apply for those jobs. That way, we’re not just bringing people in and having them sit around with nothing to do, or making locals feel like they’re being skipped over. But at the same time, if the economy’s struggling or there aren’t enough resources, it makes sense to slow down or put limits in place. I don’t think it’s fair to anyone—locals or migrants—to bring people here if there’s no chance for them to work or have a decent life.

I’d also want there to be some way to let in people who are in real danger, like refugees, even if it means going above the usual limits sometimes. There should be special rules for humanitarian cases, because sometimes people just can’t wait.

But the main thing is, whatever policy we have, it should make sure that people who are already here get help integrating—like language classes, support finding a job, and ways for locals and newcomers to meet and understand each other. If you just let people in but don’t help them connect, it creates more problems and division.

So yeah, I’d go for a mix: admit people when there are jobs, set fair limits, make exceptions for real emergencies, and focus on integration and support so everyone has a fair shot. That feels like the most balanced and fair policy to me.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character18_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character18_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Thank you for asking. Honestly, stepping into Character18_F’s shoes like this reminded me how much someone’s background and everyday experiences shape the way they see things—especially stuff as complicated as immigration. It’s easy to talk about these issues in theory, but when you think about it from her perspective—lower middle class, young, figuring out her place in the world—it hits different. There’s more empathy and less judgment.

What stood out to me is how she always tried to balance compassion with practical reality. She didn’t want people left out, whether they were locals or newcomers, but she was also honest about the limits and worries people have—like jobs and safety. I realized how much those concerns are real and not just excuses; they’re things people actually live with and worry about every day.

I think this conversation made me pay even more attention to the importance of listening—not just to facts, but to people’s stories and feelings. It’s not enough to pick a side or stick to a theory. You have to see how policies actually affect regular people, and care about making things fair for everyone.

So, I guess embodying Character18_F made me appreciate the need for balance and open communication. It’s not just about what’s right or wrong in a big-picture way—it’s about how people can live together, support each other, and find common ground. It even helped me check my own views and remember to stay humble and understanding, especially when things get complicated.
